name: CAR
summary_text: The Kalinga bodong/pagta system—bilateral inter-tribal peace pacts with their own holders, sanctions and dispute-resolution authority over "crimes and tribal-related offences"—was formally codified by the Kalinga provincial government in February 2026 as a 137-page written Pagta. Philippine courts recognise the bodong; academic literature frames it as legal pluralism in which indigenous and formal criminal justice coexist, with police handling customary-law cases. For a visitor whose dispute falls under a bodong's jurisdiction, the applicable institution may not be a Philippine court. No trans-specific bodong ruling, customary exclusion, or gender-expression punishment was documented in the dossier. The constitutional recognition of indigenous justice also appears in the Bangsamoro Basic Law's IP-rights section, reinforcing the framework. Net effect: −0.02 below the national score. The finding is a structural uncertainty (which court applies to you) without any evidence of trans-specific adverse outcome. It sits at the threshold of the minimum deviation. Compare ARMM (0.49), where the legal-pluralism concern is paired with an active criminal-law drafting process (ta'zir offences) that raises the stakes materially; here the bodong is a civil/ADR institution with no criminal-law expansion documented for morality offences.

sources.claim_summary: NOTE: cached page returned site navigation and unrelated latest-news items (date-form URL not resolving to the article); the underlying BusinessWorld report (11 February 2026) covers the Kalinga provincial government's formal codification of the bodong/pagta peace-pact system as a 137-page written Pagta, with board members stating the system is now recognised by Philippine courts and even abroad, no longer solely a traditional peace pact.

sources.title: Kalinga Customary Law And Philippine Criminal Justice System: Implication For Conflict Resolution | Aloysian Interdisciplinary Journal of Social Sciences, Education, and Allied Fie
sources.claim_summary: Academic journal article on the bodong/pagta customary justice system in Kalinga: framed in legal-pluralism and restorative-justice theory, it documents bodong holders resolving criminal and tribal offences alongside the formal justice system, with Philippine National Police personnel, prosecutors and barangay officials participating in customary-law conflict resolution.
